A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same contamination-and-forgetting study. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, allowing relocated content and substantive revisions to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training, contamination, forgetting, and weight-decay experiments in Sections 4–5, plus duplicate-filtering validation in Appendix A.3.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional OLMo-7B experiments, extended OLMo-1B results, and revised weight-decay experiments, including an appendix ablation without weight decay.

M1.justification: The exact-contamination and duplicate-filtering framework, standard language-model training, and likelihood-based evaluation are retained. Larger model configurations and weight-decay interventions change the experiments, without introducing a proposed algorithm, architecture component, loss, or inference procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same pretraining data sources, seven-benchmark mixture in Section 3.2 and Table 2, and four OLMo benchmarks: HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, and PiQA. Additional model sizes and optimizer configurations retain the represented data and tasks.

E2.justification: Both versions measure contamination against holdout questions or uncontaminated model controls. No competing comparison algorithm is introduced or removed; the new weight-decay configurations are experimental ablations.

E3.justification: v3 adds a 1.6B Chinchilla-scaled condition and OLMo-7B continual pretraining from step 300,000. OLMo-1B follow-up is extended from a reported 0.5% to 1% of remaining training. Section 5.2 replaces the 0.01/0.1/1 weight-decay sweep with interventions at a common contaminated checkpoint using 0.1/1/5/50; Appendix Figure 8 additionally tests zero weight decay.

E4.justification: The weight-decay analysis is redesigned to isolate its causal effect by continuing from the same contaminated checkpoint. New Figure 8 tests whether weight decay is necessary and shows substantial forgetting without it. The novel-data, repeated-data, contamination-position, and duplicate-filtering analyses are retained; the earlier OLMo-1B empirical-versus-decay overlay is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report bootstrapped 90% confidence intervals for the principal contamination plots and 95% intervals for duplicate-filtering validation. No new repeated-run counts, seeds, or statistical estimation procedures are documented. Additional significance statements concern new outcomes.

E6.justification: The retained 1.6B/7B-token plot changes: its four-repetition accuracy gap rises from roughly 19 to 29 points, although v3 Section 4.1 still says 20. Table 1 adds a 1.6B row, including 52.06% holdout and 67.61% four-repetition accuracy. New OLMo-7B results report a 17-point contamination increase and 87% reduction after 13% of remaining training. Extended OLMo-1B results report 96% reduction after 1%, versus 84% after 0.5% in v1. Weight-decay result curves also change.

T1.justification: v3 removes v1 Appendix A.5's projection-based forgetting definition, two orthogonality assumptions, and Proposition 3 with its proof. It corrects the gradient-expansion sign and cumulative-product indexing. The retained decay proposition becomes an explicit sufficient bound, proved using log(1−x) ≤ −x instead of the earlier small-x approximation.

C1.justification: v1's abstract advertises a theory bounding example-forgetting time for any training run with known AdamW hyperparameters. v3 replaces that advertised guarantee with an empirical relationship between forgetting and cumulative weight decay. This substantially narrows a central theoretical contribution while retaining the main conclusion that contamination can be forgotten.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly recognizes influence through subsequent gradient trajectories and makes large-model forgetting estimates conditional on an empirical hypothesis. It adds that weight decay is unnecessary for forgetting and interprets OLMo-7B forgetting as slower than OLMo-1B. It also removes v1's learning-rate tuning recommendation and categorical dismissal of individual-data attribution in the forgetting regime.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.4 provides a paper-specific code link, explicit codebase and dataset access links, and a reproducibility statement covering contamination positions. It discloses 8×A100 training hardware and three weeks on an 8×H100 node for OLMo-7B. v1 names underlying tools and data but lacks this project-code access and computational-resource documentation.

R1.justification: The same 74 references and substantive related-work discussion are retained. The relationships to contamination detection, natural forgetting, and data attribution research remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Section 5 is extensively rewritten and reorganized into cumulative decay, controlled empirical evaluation, and conditional large-scale extrapolation. The abstract, introductory contribution discussion, Section 4.3, and discussion are revised accordingly. The appendix structure changes through replacement of the extended theoretical analysis with reproducibility information and supplementary experiments.

P2.justification: The duplicate-question illustration and OLMo-1B plots move to the appendix, while the scaling figure moves earlier. v3 adds OLMo-7B and zero-weight-decay figures, redesigns the weight-decay panels and axes, and extends the Chinchilla plot. Table 1 is expanded and reformatted, and Table 2 receives rotated column headings despite retaining its data.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central weight-decay argument through controlled interventions, a zero-decay ablation, corrected mathematics, and explicit acknowledgment that gradient decay does not itself guarantee example forgetting. OLMo-7B evidence and new reproducibility information further strengthen the paper. The formal scope is narrower and large-scale extrapolation remains hypothetical; the revised scaling plot also conflicts with unchanged prose. These reporting limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and qualification of the conclusions.
